extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, geometers, and readers evaluating claims about quadrature of the circle
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing arguments, constructions, and demonstrations offered as proofs of a definable relation between a circle's diameter and circumference (the quadrature problem). Includes geometric construction checks, arithmetic consistency, and empirical/experimental tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate hypothesis before deducing conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writer must be good enough to give a demonstration of the truth of his hypothesis, before he expects me to admit conclusions based upon it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base further conclusions on an assumed relation between diameter and circumference: any asserted value (e.g., that circumference = 3.125 × diameter) must be demonstrated. If you present a hypothesis about the circle you must supply a proof or demonstration rather than using the hypothesis as a premise for successive deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on truncated interminable decimals as exact values
rubrics_metrics.description: “3.4342… is an interminable decimal fraction, and is less than the true value of D H; and .5658 is greater than the true value of H G; and by your mode of calculation this false value … you thus get a false value … and at every successive step this becomes an increasing error.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intermediate geometrical lengths are represented by terminating/truncated decimals taken from infinite expansions, truncation can introduce errors that propagate and grow in subsequent constructions. Proofs that treat such truncations as exact must be treated as fallacious or at least require justification of error control/convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/ocular demonstration is a valid test
rubrics_metrics.description: E. M. suggests measuring a large circle’s semi-circumference to show that a proposed ratio (e.g., 3.125) is inconsistent with direct measurement: “The proposal was to measure a radius of 100 feet, and to describe a semi-circumference, in order by measurement of the latter to prove ocularly, that its length is greater than 312·5 feet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed exact relation between diameter and circumference should be testable by sufficiently accurate physical measurement. If an experiment (e.g., drawing a large circle and measuring its semi-circumference) contradicts the proposed ratio, that provides a practical refutation. When invoking experiment, ensure measurement precision and control of construction error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations among constructed figures must be expressible in finite terms
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a perfect relation between all these geometrical figures, which can be expressed in finite terms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer demonstrations that exhibit exact, finite algebraic/geometric relations between constructed squares, triangles, and circles rather than relying solely on infinite processes or non-finite symbolic representations. If you claim finite expressibility, produce the explicit finite relations or constructions that realize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume mutually inconsistent numerical assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: “You may assume the diameter to equal 1, or, you may assume the circumference to equal 3·125, but you must not assume both values simultaneously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making simultaneous assumptions that are logically contradictory (e.g., assigning both a fixed diameter and a fixed numerical circumference that the diameter would not imply). When testing a proposed ratio, choose a consistent normalization (fix diameter or circumference) and check consequences consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard polygon-approximation claim: circle area is intermediate between inscribed and circumscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar mode of proof: inscribe and circumscribe regular polygons and let the number of sides increase; the circle’s area lies between the polygonal bounds and in the limit equals their common limit (the usual derivation of π decimals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical justification for limits producing the area/circumference of a circle. If relying on this method, one should justify the limiting argument (convergence of polygon areas/perimeters to the circle’s area/perimeter). Note the page contains dispute about whether the circle’s area is legitimately 'intermediate' in a finite sense without invoking limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale invariance: a property found for one circle applies universally
rubrics_metrics.description: E. M.: “The property of one circle is the property of all circles, and if there is any circle whose radius is 1, and whose semi-circumference is greater than 3·125 … then in all circles the ratio … is greater…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about ratios (circumference/diameter), use homogeneity: geometric ratios are scale-invariant. A counterexample at one scale (if correctly constructed) suffices to refute a universal numeric claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: A given perimeter form (circumference) cannot be made to contain arbitrary different areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith’s elastic-line thought experiment: a line of fixed length (e.g., 32 inches) laid out as different rectangles does not in general produce the same area; equivalently, the circle’s circumference uniquely bounds its maximal enclosed area among shapes of given perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject arguments that treat perimeter-length alone as freely reassignable to produce equal areas in different shapes. Use isoperimetric reasoning: for fixed perimeter, the circle maximizes enclosed area; one cannot arbitrarily reshape a closed line to produce the same area as the circle unless consistent with geometric constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arithmetic mean and algebraic root relations carefully to relate areas and diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith repeatedly forms expressions like 0.5625 + 1 = 1.5625, notes square roots (√0.5625 = 0.75, √1.5625 = 1.25) and uses the arithmetical mean of roots to infer diameters: “the arithmetical mean between .75 and 1·25 is unity … equal to the diameter of the smaller circles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using mean/root manipulations to deduce linear measures from areas, state assumptions clearly (e.g., which areas correspond to which circles) and show algebraic steps. Verify that root-extractions and averaging operations are valid in the given geometric context and do not conflate units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify iterative/infinite constructions and their consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith describes repeating constructions inward/outward 'ad infinitum' producing sequences of squares and circles related by simple factors and claims arithmetic consistency across iterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an argument depends on repeating a construction indefinitely, either provide a finite invariant or prove properties of the infinite sequence (limit or closed-form relation). Check that every step is well-defined and that accumulated operations preserve the asserted relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat linear and square units distinctly and correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith acknowledges being accused of treating linear and square units as identical and defends his usage while noting the charge: “One of your charges against me is, that of treating linear and square units as if they were identical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about units: when moving between lengths and areas (e.g., relating diameter to area of a square), maintain correct dimensional analysis. Avoid arguments that implicitly equate numerical values of lengths and areas without proper interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using polygonal approximation, justify passage to limit (convergence) and explain possible paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith critiques the usual polygonal argument by claiming the inscribed polygon has smaller perimeter and cannot be made to contain the same area as a circle, and warns of deriving exact irrational values from finitely-described polygons without addressing infinite decimal behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you rely on inscribed/circumscribed polygons to establish circle area or circumference, provide a clear limiting argument: show polygon perimeters/areas converge monotonically to the circle’s values and control errors. Explicitly address how infinite digits/irrationalities are handled and why truncation does not produce logical contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check geometric equalities by independent constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith repeatedly cross-checks values via multiple constructions (squares on triangle sides, inscribed hexagon/dodecagon, diagonals equal to diameters) to confirm consistency: 'we obtain arithmetical values for every line in the diagram, thoroughly consistent with what every Mathematician must admit to be geometrically true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate claimed equalities by constructing alternative, independent geometric derivations of the same quantity (e.g., obtain a diameter from a diagonal in a square and from a side of an inscribed polygon). Multiple independent confirmations strengthen a proposed relation.
